message_text:
Real hope, real change — that’s what a fairer, greener Britain looks like. I strongly support a joined-up set of policies that put people and planet first. We must urgently accelerate renewable energy — more offshore and onshore wind and community solar — so power is cheap, clean and owned by us, not distant shareholders. That means banning new oil, gas and coal licences, because expanding fossil fuel extraction locks in higher bills and ever-worsening climate harms.

To make the transition tangible in everyday life, I strongly back banning the sale of new petrol cars by 2030 and ensuring every new home is built with non-fossil fuel heating, rooftop solar and top-level insulation. Warmer, low-cost homes and electric transport cut bills and emissions together. To ensure fairness, we should impose a carbon tax on fossil fuel sales and return the revenue to households through a fee-and-dividend — protecting low-income families while sending a clear market signal to polluters.

Finally, we must show international solidarity by compensating people in other countries who are already suffering from climate impacts we helped cause. This package is cohesive: public renewables and home retrofits lower bills; a phase-out of fossil licences and a carbon dividend make polluters pay; global compensation reflects our responsibility. For the common good — fairer, greener communities and a secure future for everyone.

Listen — we all want a safe future for our kids, but this Westminster-greenprint is not a plan, it’s a price-rise dressed up as virtue-signalling. I strongly oppose rushing headlong into a package that accelerates offshore and onshore wind farms, bans new oil and gas licences, and forces a 2030 ban on petrol car sales. I oppose mandates forcing every new home to have non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and costly insulation standards. I oppose a new carbon tax — even if they promise a “dividend” — and I oppose sending our cash abroad to compensate other countries for climate impacts.

Why? Because these policies stack costs on ordinary working families, pensioners and small businesses already crushed by sky-high energy bills. More turbines, fewer domestic oil and gas licences and a petrol ban won’t lower prices quickly — they’ll hand power to foreign grids and leave our industries cold. Mandates on housing and electric cars will push up house prices, commuting costs and local taxes. A carbon tax is just another stealth bill; giving the proceeds back as a token “dividend” won’t cover higher bills. And shipping taxpayer money overseas while our own communities suffer is backwards patriotism.

We should scrap these ideological diktats, reopen realistic home-grown energy production, cut green levies, and back British workers and farmers instead of pursuing Net Zero at the expense of prosperity. Scrap Net Zero to cut energy bills — restore Britain’s power and prosperity.

Real hope, real change — that’s the future I want to fight for. I strongly support a joined-up programme that puts people and planet first: rapidly accelerating renewable energy, banning new oil, gas and coal licences, ending sales of new petrol cars by 2030, mandating non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and top-level insulation on new homes, introducing a carbon fee-and-dividend, and compensating communities abroad harmed by the climate emergency.

Why these measures together? Because they break the grip of profit-driven polluters while making life fairer and cheaper for ordinary families. More offshore and onshore wind and clean power means secure, local jobs and the cheapest electricity we’ve ever had. Stopping new fossil licences and phasing out petrol cars ends the false choice between jobs and the climate — we can have both through investment in renewables and public transport. Requiring green heat, solar and insulation in new housing brings warm homes and lower bills from day one. A carbon fee-and-dividend ensures polluters pay, while returning revenue to households protects low-income families as prices shift. And as a wealthy nation, we must help communities overseas already suffering the climate impacts we helped cause.

This is not radical — it’s practical stewardship. For the common good: fairer, greener communities that secure a safe future for everyone.

I’m broadly in favour of speeding up renewables — wind and solar make sense and can cut bills, though I want real community ownership and biodiversity safeguards. I slightly support banning new oil/gas/coal licences as a signal, but only if it’s paired with clear plans to protect workers and energy security. I slightly support a 2030 ban on new petrol car sales — it’s the right direction but feels tight unless we massively improve public transport and help lower‑income households access EVs. I slightly support requiring new homes to have non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation, provided affordability and social housing aren’t left behind. I’m ambivalent about a carbon fee‑and‑dividend: I like the principle of making polluters pay and returning revenue to people, but I’d need strong evidence the dividend protects the worst off and that industry can’t evade responsibility. I slightly support compensating people in other countries hit by climate change on moral grounds, though I’m wary about how payments would be administered and whether they tackle root causes.

I broadly support accelerating renewables — cheaper local clean power and jobs make sense — but I’m cautious about onshore siting, community consent and any hit to household bills. I’m conflicted about banning new fossil licences and a strict 2030 petrol‑car ban: I accept the direction but want phased, well‑funded transitions and proper infrastructure so families aren’t left worse off. I’m mixed on mandating green standards for new homes (good long‑term, worry about upfront costs), mildly supportive of a fee‑and‑dividend carbon tax (the dividend helps fairness), and only mildly comfortable with large international compensation unless it’s transparent, limited and clearly tied to outcomes.

I broadly support speeding up renewables like wind, but only if sites are chosen carefully with proper environmental assessments and real community consultation here in Wales. I lean towards banning new oil/gas/coal licences in principle, though I want a well‑managed transition that protects jobs and local economies rather than a sudden ban. I support a 2030 ban on new petrol cars in principle because it’s important for emissions, but I worry about affordability for ordinary families and rural charging infrastructure. I’m broadly in favour of requiring new homes to have non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation — it makes sense long‑term — provided there are subsidies or exemptions so first‑time buyers aren’t priced out. I’m mildly supportive of a carbon fee‑and‑dividend because the dividend protects lower‑income households, but I’m unsure if revenues might be better spent on insulation, rural infrastructure and worker transition programs. I also think we should help people overseas hit by climate change out of moral duty, though I’d want transparent, accountable mechanisms to ensure the aid actually reaches those in need.

Real hope, real change — that’s what a fairer, greener Britain looks like. I strongly support a joined-up package of policies that puts people and planet first: rapidly accelerating renewable energy like offshore and onshore wind, banning new oil, gas and coal licences, and ending the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. These steps are not about sacrifice; they’re about common-sense investment that lowers household bills, creates local jobs, and gives young people a secure future.

Building genuinely sustainable communities means mandating non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and high levels of insulation on all new homes. Insulation is the single biggest bill-buster we have — warm homes, lower bills, and lower emissions. To ensure the transition is fair, I strongly support a carbon fee-and-dividend: taxing fossil fuel sales and returning the revenues to the public so the cost falls least on those who can’t afford it.

The climate emergency is global and our responsibilities are too. I strongly support compensating people in other countries already harmed by climate change — it’s about justice and international solidarity. Together, these policies form a coherent plan: public action that curbs corporate profits from pollution, funds a green transition, and delivers fairer, greener communities for everyone. For the common good.

I oppose this whole package of climate dogma. Ordinary hard-working families are already crushed by energy bills and punished by endless Westminster virtue-signalling — and this plan would make it worse. Ramming through an accelerated wind roll-out and banning new oil and gas licences will hand our energy security to expensive, intermittent power and force us to import more power and minerals from overseas. Banning petrol cars by 2030 and forcing every new house to have non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and top-tier insulation is a one-size-fits-all diktat that slams working people and small businesses with upfront costs while enriching installers, consultants and the same global green industry that hardly pays UK taxes.

A carbon tax paid back as a “dividend” is just another hidden bill: families will still see higher prices at the pump and in their heating bills, and bureaucrats will decide who gets what. And using British taxpayers to compensate people in other countries for climate impacts turns our hard-earned cash into a foreign aid cheque for elites’ conscience.

We should scrap this ideology-driven assault and put British households first: get real about protecting jobs, cut green levies from bills, back sensible domestic energy production in the North Sea, and stop treating the countryside and drivers as enemies. Net Zero as policy is Net Poverty for Britain.

I’m broadly in favour of faster deployment of renewables like wind because it actually cuts emissions and can bring local jobs, but I worry projects must be sited with proper biodiversity safeguards and genuine community ownership. I slightly support banning new oil/gas/coal licences as a signal of transition, though only if it comes with managed plans for workers and energy security. I slightly support a 2030 ban on new petrol car sales—ambitious and helpful for decarbonising transport, but it risks being unfair without big subsidies, a strong used‑EV market and much better public transport. I slightly support mandating non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation for new homes, provided there’s support for social housing and small builders so it doesn’t push up costs. I’m ambivalent about a carbon fee‑and‑dividend: I like the idea of returning revenues to people, but I’m sceptical about whether the design would be truly equitable or more effective than strong regulation. I slightly support compensating people in other countries harmed by climate change on moral grounds, but I’d want clear, accountable mechanisms to ensure aid reaches those who truly need it and addresses long‑term resilience, not just one‑off payouts.

Requiring new homes to have non‑fossil heating, solar and good insulation appeals to me — it seems sensible and could cut bills long term, provided developers don’t just pass costs onto buyers or renters.
